challenges.claim: A ledger shows lawmakers' funds sent to groups that cannot be found. Which source should you NOT trust?
options: The Commission on Audit's published report, listing each group and its address
A cropped screenshot from an anonymous chat, with no author or date
A police report of a visit to the listed addresses, signed and dated
challenges.explanation: A screenshot with no author, date or original source cannot be checked. Official records and audit reports can be traced back to who published them.

challenges.claim: A photo is said to show the Fund Fixer having lunch with a lawmaker's chief of staff. Which statement about it is unreliable?
options: The photo's metadata shows the date and place, matching the restaurant's own post
A post says 'everyone knows this is the chief of staff' but gives no name or source
A news outlet identified both people and named its source
challenges.explanation: 'Everyone knows' is a rumor, not a source. A claim should name who said it and how they know.

challenges.claim: Messages seem to arrange a share of each fund release. Which source is the fake or unreliable one?
options: Messages retrieved with a court order and entered as evidence
A signed statement from the NGO's owner confirming the messages are real
A typed 'transcript' of the messages posted by an account created yesterday
challenges.explanation: A new account posting a retyped transcript could have changed the words. Original, authenticated messages are far more trustworthy.

challenges.claim: A spokesperson says the Secretary 'fully supports' the bill, quoting one line. Which version should you NOT trust?
options: The full original statement published on the agency's own site
One line cut from the middle of the statement, shared without the rest
The agency's official transcript of the press briefing
challenges.explanation: A single cut-out line can reverse a meaning. Check the full original, with its date and author.

challenges.claim: A page says thousands of citizens support the project. Which source is unreliable?
options: Hundreds of posts from brand-new accounts that all repeat the same sentence
A signed petition whose names were verified by the city clerk
A survey that publishes its method and sample size
challenges.explanation: Many new accounts repeating one sentence look like a coordinated campaign, not real people. Verified signatures and open methods can be checked.

challenges.claim: A video seems to show the official saying nothing was wrong. What should you NOT trust?
options: The full, unedited recording from the broadcaster's archive
A short clip with jump cuts and no source, reposted by an anonymous account
The broadcaster's published editing log
challenges.explanation: Jump cuts and a missing source mean you cannot tell what was left out. Go back to the full original recording.

challenges.claim: Envelopes of cash are marked with voters' names. Which source should you NOT trust?
options: A handwritten note from a poll watcher, with the date, time, place and a phone number to call
A polished 'Election Integrity Bureau' statement with a seal that says the envelopes are fake, with no author or evidence
A police inventory of the envelopes, signed and dated at the scene
challenges.explanation: A seal and a fancy name prove nothing. The plain handwritten note can be checked: it says who, when and where, and gives a way to ask. A report with no author and no evidence cannot be checked.

challenges.claim: Receipts show voters were paid for proof of their ballot. Which source is unreliable?
options: A neatly designed 'Citizens' Watch' summary saying 'receipts were forged by the opposition', with no names or numbers
A receipt book obtained by the election commission, with serial numbers
A shaky phone recording of a voter describing the payment, with the voter's name and barangay on file
challenges.explanation: Good design is not good evidence. The summary names nobody and gives no numbers. The shaky recording and the numbered receipts both lead to real people and records.

challenges.claim: A poll says 98% of voters support the campaign. Which source is the unreliable one?
options: An independent poll with a different result and a public method
A university study presented on a glossy poster, quoting '98%' with no sample size or method
A photocopied page from a local pollster listing how many people were asked and how they were chosen
challenges.explanation: A glossy poster is not a method. A photocopied page that shows who was asked and how can be checked, even if it looks plain.

challenges.claim: A file says a relative was hired with no interview. What should you NOT trust?
options: A formal letter on 'Office of Good Governance' paper saying 'all hiring was fair', unsigned and undated
The personnel office's own signed hiring record
A coffee-stained notebook kept by the receptionist, with dates and names of every interview held that year
challenges.explanation: Official-looking paper does not make a claim true. An unsigned, undated letter cannot be traced. The messy notebook and the signed record both name dates and people.

challenges.claim: A ranked list shows the person hired placed last. Which source is unreliable?
options: A clean, printed list from 'the Director's office' with no signatures and scores in a different font
The ranking sheet signed by the three-person panel
A crumpled copy of the same sheet kept by one panelist, with their signature and the date
challenges.explanation: A tidy list with mismatched fonts and no signatures may have been edited. A crumpled copy is still signed, so it can be compared with the panel's own sheet.

challenges.claim: Payroll records list relatives paid for jobs with no duties. Which source is unreliable?
options: A spreadsheet screenshot with the Treasury logo, no title, date or file name
The auditor's report that matches each name to a job description
A scruffy photocopy of the payroll with department codes and the treasury clerk's initials
challenges.explanation: A logo is easy to paste on a screenshot. With no title, date or file name it cannot be traced. The scruffy photocopy has codes and initials someone can verify.

challenges.claim: A photo shows the flood wall was never built. Which source should you NOT trust?
options: A blurry phone photo from a passing driver, with its date and GPS place in the file details
A glossy brochure from the Public Works Office showing an artist's drawing of 'the completed flood wall', with no photos of the site
The inspector's signed site report with the date of the visit
challenges.explanation: A drawing is not proof that anything exists. The blurry photo is ugly but its date and place can be checked, and so can the signed report.

challenges.claim: Invoices show steel bars bought at ten times the market price. Which source is unreliable?
options: A price list on the supplier's letterhead saying 'our prices are always fair', with no dates or item numbers
The invoices themselves, with numbers and the Public Works Office's stamp
A pencil-written comparison by a junior accountant listing three other shops' prices with their phone numbers
challenges.explanation: A seller saying its own prices are fair is not a check. The pencil comparison gives shops anyone can call, and the numbered invoices can be matched to payments.

challenges.claim: A registry card shows the winning company was founded a week before the bid. Which source is unreliable?
options: A company website with a professional photo of 'our 30-year history', with no registration number
The government business registry entry with the founding date and the owner's name
A faded newspaper notice of the company's founding, with the date and the paper's stamp
challenges.explanation: A website can say anything about its own history. The registry and the old notice are kept by others, so the founding date can be compared.

challenges.claim: A budget document has the pages listing who proposed which projects blacked out. Which source should you NOT trust?
options: A grainy scan of the full budget document from before the black marker, stamped by the archive with a date
A press release called 'Transparency Report' that says 'nothing was withheld', with no copy of the budget attached
The archive's own log showing who ordered the pages blacked out
challenges.explanation: Claiming nothing was hidden is not showing it. The grainy scan and the archive log can be compared with the blacked-out copy.

challenges.claim: Three requests for public records were refused with the same one line. Which source is unreliable?
options: A hand-signed letter from a citizen listing the dates of each refused request and the refusal numbers
A friendly statement titled 'We Welcome Your Questions' with no examples of requests answered
The office's own registry showing the requests and the refusals
challenges.explanation: A welcome message is not a record. The letter and the registry give dates and numbers that others can check.

challenges.claim: A log shows four pallets of records were shredded before the audit. Which source is unreliable?
options: A spotless certificate from 'the Office of Archives' saying 'no records were destroyed', with no signature
The shredding service's signed invoice for the night, with the truck number
A night guard's note on the gate log with the time the truck left
challenges.explanation: A spotless certificate with no signature can be written by anyone. The invoice and the gate log are kept by other people and can be matched.

challenges.claim: An email lists relatives added to the payroll. Which source should you NOT trust?
options: A neat 'leaked memo' on official-looking letterhead posted by a new account, with no sender, date or file
A plain printout of the email showing sender, recipient and date, passed on by a staff member a journalist can reach
A payroll audit note that matches three of the names
challenges.explanation: Letterhead is easy to fake. The plain printout has headers that can be checked, and the audit note can be compared with the payroll.

challenges.claim: A former fund clerk's statement says public money went to dummy groups. Which source should you NOT trust?
options: A statement sworn before a notary, with the clerk's name and signature
An 'official denial' on Fund Office letterhead, unsigned and undated
A diary page with dates and amounts that match the ledger
challenges.explanation: A denial nobody signed or dated cannot be questioned. A sworn statement and a diary with checkable amounts can.

challenges.claim: A whistleblower's folder lists who asked for which projects. Which source is unreliable?
options: A 'leak' posted by a brand-new account that says 'it is all in the files', with nothing attached
Emails and lists whose dates match the official budget records
A printout passed through a lawyer who can confirm where it came from
challenges.explanation: A claim with nothing attached proves nothing. Files that match the official records, and a lawyer who vouches for the source, can be checked.
